label: Opposite gender word by faith
summary: Gives "women" or "men", whichever is the gender opposite to the one that dominates the character's faith.
details: If the faith's dominant gender is male (or equal), the text is "women". If it is female (or equal), the text is "men". The first matching entry wins, so with an equal faith you get "women". The game marks it as usable for random text picks.

label: Wrestling style name
summary: Gives the name of a regional wrestling style, chosen by the character's culture.
details: Iranian heritage gives Koshti, Burman gives Naban, any Germanic heritage gives Ringen, Indo-Aryan or Dravidian gives Malla-yuddha, Yoruba gives a Yoruba style, and everything else gets a fallback. The input shows the text of only the first four.

label: Writing material
summary: Gives the name of a writing material that fits the region where the character is.
details: Examples: parchment in Europe and the Middle East, papyrus in Egypt, palm leaf in India and Southeast Asia, stone stele on the steppe, paper in China, Japan and Korea. Birch bark is the fallback. The regions overlap (Europe also fits vellum), and the game may pick randomly among the entries that fit.

label: Writing material, plural
summary: Gives the plural of the writing material that fits the region where the character is, such as parchments, papyri or palm leaves.
details: It uses the same region rules and the same seven materials as the singular text, so use the same region for both if a sentence needs both. The game may pick randomly among the entries that fit.

label: Young, middle-aged or old
summary: Gives "young", "middle-aged" or "old" for the character's age.
details: Age 30 or less is young, above 30 and below 60 is middle-aged, and 60 or more is old.

label: Younger or older than other
summary: Gives "young" if the character is younger than the other person in the text (`second`), and "old" if they are the same age or older.
details: It compares two people, not a fixed age limit, so the other person must be set as `second`.

label: Consort type to other
summary: Gives the word for the tie between the character and the other person (`second`): wife, husband, betrothed, concubinist, concubine, soulmate, lover or, failing all of those, good friend.
details: Wife and husband need the two to be married, and follow the character's sex. The other words come from the betrothed, concubine, soulmate and lover relations, checked in that order, and "good friend" is the fallback. The input shows the text of only the first four entries.

label: Girl or boy
summary: Gives "girl" for a female character and "boy" for a male one.

label: Girls or boys
summary: Gives "girls" for a female character and "boys" for a male one.
details: The sex is the character's own, not a group's. The entries point to the game's own words for girls and boys.

label: Girl's or boy's
summary: Gives "girl's" for a female character and "boy's" for a male one.

label: Girls, boys or children
summary: Gives "girls" if the character and the other person (`second`) are both female, "boys" if both are male, and "children" otherwise.
details: The word names the pair as a group, so it needs `second` to be set.

label: Good or bad
summary: Gives "good" if the character has the flag `good_thing_flag`, and "bad" if they have `bad_thing_flag`.
details: With neither flag, no entry fits. The game marks it as usable for random text picks.

label: Childhood study outcome
summary: Gives a short sentence about how a child fared in one field of study, depending on whether their childhood trait suited it and how far they got.
details: There are 30 entries: five fields (martial, diplomacy, stewardship, intrigue, learning), each for a childhood trait that suited the field (affinity), one that did not (disaffinity) or neither, and for a good or a bad outcome. The outcome is good when the character has the matching education trait at rank 3 or more, and bad at rank 1 or 2. The texts name the child and use her/his words. The input shows only the first 12 entry names and four texts.

label: Guild type (event 1041)
summary: Gives "Blacksmiths' Guild" or "Merchants' Guild" for a title, depending on which guild modifier its county has.
details: It runs on a title. A county with the blacksmiths' guild modifier gives the blacksmiths' text; the merchants' text is the fallback. The entry names say 1040 although the key says 1041.

label: Out of wedlock (event 1055)
summary: Gives the words " out of wedlock" when the character is neither married nor a concubine, and nothing otherwise.
details: The first entry starts with a space so it can be placed straight after another word. The second entry is empty.

label: Client type (event 1062)
summary: Gives "gardener", "court poet" or "natural philosopher", depending on which of three flags the character has.
details: The flags are governance_1062_gardener_flag, governance_1062_poet_flag and governance_1062_philosopher_flag. The poet is also the fallback. The text is lowercase, for use inside a sentence; the capitalised key is for titles.

label: Client type, capitalised
summary: Gives "Gardener", "Court Poet" or "Natural Philosopher" with capital letters, from the same three flags as the lowercase key.
details: Meant for headings and titles; the lowercase key fits inside a sentence.

label: Opening for ceremonial liege
summary: Gives the start of a greeting such as "Greetings, [titled name]," to the other person (`second`).
details: A speaker whose faith belongs to the Islamic religion gets the "As-salaam alaykum" form. Everyone else gets the plain "Greetings". Its name matches the greeting_ceremonial_liege_fallback entry of the liege greeting, which vanilla uses when the greeted person is a ceremonial regent.

label: Opening for liked regent
summary: Gives a warm greeting such as "Greetings, most [compliment word] [titled name]," to the other person (`second`).
details: A compliment word is added in front of the name. A speaker of the Islamic religion gets the "As-salaam alaykum" form, others the plain "Greetings". It goes with the liked-liege greeting for a ceremonial regent.

label: Opening for liked child
summary: Gives a warm greeting to a child, such as "Greetings, my dear daughter," or "son".
details: The other person (`second`) is the child, and the word daughter or son comes from a further text. A speaker of the Islamic religion gets the "As-salaam alaykum" form, others the plain "Greetings".

label: Opening for neutral child
summary: Gives a plain greeting to a child, such as "Greetings, daughter," or "son".
details: Like the liked-child opening but without "my dear". A speaker of the Islamic religion gets the "As-salaam alaykum" form, others the plain "Greetings".

label: Opening for family, plain
summary: Gives a plain greeting to a relative using the short relation word, such as "Greetings, uncle,".
details: The other person (`second`) is the relative, and the relation to the speaker is written by a further text. A speaker of the Islamic religion gets the "As-salaam alaykum" form, others the plain "Greetings".

label: Opening for liked family
summary: Gives a warm greeting to a relative, such as "My dear [relation],".
details: A speaker of the Islamic religion gets "As-salaam alaykum, my dear ...". Everyone else gets the shorter "My dear ...", with no "Greetings" in front.

label: Opening for foreign ruler
summary: Gives a neutral opening for a foreign ruler, such as "Peace be upon you," or "God keep you,", followed by their name.
details: The opening follows the speaker's faith or culture: Islam gives "As-salaam alaykum" (twice as likely) or "Peace be upon you"; Christianity "God's blessing upon thee" or "God keep you"; Judaism "Shalom" or a high god's guidance; Zoroastrianism a light greeting; Hinduism a dharma greeting. Germanic polytheists say "Hail", other polytheists invoke the gods' protection, and cultures with an Asian heritage pillar invoke the heavens. A plain greeting is the fallback. When several fit, the game picks randomly.

label: Opening for ordinary person
summary: Gives a neutral opening for a person with no special tie, such as "Peace be upon you," or "Hail,", followed by their name.
details: It follows the same faith and culture rules as the foreign-ruler opening, with the same twelve entries. Only the greeted person's name is written differently.

label: Opening for liked liege
summary: Gives a warm greeting to a liege, such as "Greetings, my [compliment word] liege,".
details: A speaker of the Islamic religion gets the "As-salaam alaykum" form, others the plain "Greetings".

label: Opening for liked liege, regent form
summary: Gives a warm greeting that uses the title of the speaker's top liege, such as "Greetings, [compliment word] [title],".
details: A speaker of the Islamic religion gets the "As-salaam alaykum" form, others the plain "Greetings". The input does not show where vanilla uses it, so the "regent" in its name is not explained.

label: Opening for neutral liege
summary: Gives a neutral greeting that ends in "my liege,", with an opening chosen by the speaker's faith or culture.
details: The rules are the same as for the foreign-ruler opening: Islam, Christianity, Judaism, Zoroastrianism, Hinduism, Germanic or other polytheists and cultures with an Asian heritage pillar each have their own opening. A plain one is the fallback, and there are ten entries in all. When several fit, the game picks randomly.

label: Opening for neutral liege, regent form
summary: Gives a neutral greeting that uses the title of the speaker's top liege, such as "Greetings, [title],".
details: A speaker of the Islamic religion gets the "As-salaam alaykum" form, others the plain "Greetings". The input does not show where vanilla uses it, so the "regent" in its name is not explained.

label: Opening for lover, plain
summary: Gives a greeting to a lover, such as "[Titled name], my dear [pet name],".
details: A speaker of the Islamic religion gets "As-salaam alaykum" in front. Others start directly with the name. The pet name comes from a further text.

label: Opening for liked parent
summary: Gives a warm greeting to a parent, such as "Greetings, dear mother," or "father".
details: Mother or father comes from a further text for the other person (`second`). A speaker of the Islamic religion gets the "As-salaam alaykum" form, others the plain "Greetings".

label: Opening for neutral parent
summary: Gives a plain greeting to a parent, such as "Greetings, mother,".
details: Like the liked-parent opening without "dear". A speaker of the Islamic religion gets the "As-salaam alaykum" form, others the plain "Greetings".

label: Opening for liked sibling
summary: Gives a warm greeting to a sibling, such as "Greetings, my dear sister," or "brother".
details: Sister or brother comes from a further text for the other person (`second`). A speaker of the Islamic religion gets the "As-salaam alaykum" form, others the plain "Greetings".

label: Opening for neutral sibling
summary: Gives a plain greeting to a sibling, such as "Greetings, sister," or "brother".
details: Like the liked-sibling opening without "my dear". A speaker of the Islamic religion gets the "As-salaam alaykum" form, others the plain "Greetings".

label: Opening for liked spouse
summary: Gives a warm greeting to a spouse, such as "Greetings, my cherished wife," or "husband".
details: Wife or husband comes from the other person (`second`). A speaker of the Islamic religion gets the "As-salaam alaykum" form, others the plain "Greetings".

label: Opening for neutral spouse
summary: Gives a plain greeting to a spouse, such as "Greetings, my wife," or "husband".
details: Like the liked-spouse opening, with "my" instead of "my cherished". A speaker of the Islamic religion gets the "As-salaam alaykum" form, others the plain "Greetings".

label: Greeting to family
summary: Gives a greeting from the speaker to a relative, chosen by how much the speaker likes them.
details: If the speaker's opinion of the relative (`second`) is 40 or more, the greeting is the warm one. At -20 or less it is the cold one. Anything in between gives the fallback. Each entry hands over to another greeting text. The cold one also ends in the fallback text.

label: Greeting to disliked family
summary: Gives the greeting for a relative the speaker dislikes, which is the plain family greeting.
details: It has only one entry, which hands over to the plain family opening ("Greetings, [relation],"). So a disliked relative gets no special insult.

label: Greeting to liked family
summary: Gives the greeting for a relative the speaker likes.
details: It has only one entry, which hands over to the liked-family opening ("My dear [relation],").

label: Greeting to foreign ruler
summary: Gives a greeting from the speaker to a foreign ruler: warm, insulting or neutral, depending on the speaker's opinion of them.
details: With an opinion of 40 or more the warm greeting is used ("To the [compliment] [name],"). At -20 or less the insulting one ("To the [insult] [titled name],"). Otherwise the neutral foreign-ruler opening is used. The greeted ruler is `second`.

label: Greeting to disliked foreign ruler
summary: Gives an insulting greeting to a foreign ruler, such as "To the [insult word] [titled name],".
details: It has one entry. The insult word comes from a further text that is given the speaker as an extra argument.

label: Greeting to liked foreign ruler
summary: Gives a warm greeting to a foreign ruler, such as "Hail and well met," or "To the [compliment word] [name],".
details: Ten entries. The compliment greeting is always allowed, and the others follow the speaker's faith or culture (Islam, Christianity, Judaism, Zoroastrianism, Hinduism, polytheists, Asian heritage). The game may pick randomly among those that fit.

label: Greeting to ordinary person
summary: Gives a greeting from the speaker to a person with no special tie: warm, insulting or neutral, depending on the speaker's opinion of them.
details: With an opinion of 40 or more the warm greeting is used ("To the [compliment] [first name],"). At -40 or less the insulting one. Otherwise the neutral generic opening is used. The greeted person is `second`.

label: Greeting to disliked person
summary: Gives an insulting greeting, such as "To the [insult word] [first name],".
details: It has one entry. The insult word comes from a further text that is given the speaker as an extra argument.

label: Greeting to liked person
summary: Gives a warm greeting to an ordinary person, such as "Hail and well met, [first name],".
details: Ten entries. The compliment greeting is always allowed, and the others follow the speaker's faith or culture. The game may pick randomly among those that fit.

label: Greeting to liege
summary: Gives the greeting the speaker uses to the other person (`second`) when that person is their liege.
details: The checks run in this order. If the liege is the speaker's parent, child, sibling or spouse, the neutral family greeting is used. Then an opinion of 20 or more gives the liked-liege greeting, and -40 or less the disliked one. Then a ceremonial regent gets the ceremonial liege fallback, and everyone else the plain liege fallback.

label: Greeting to disliked liege
summary: Gives the greeting to a liege the speaker dislikes: "To the [title]," if the liege is a ceremonial regent, otherwise "To my liege,".
details: Two entries. The liege is the other person (`second`).

label: Greeting to neutral liege
summary: Gives the greeting to a liege the speaker neither likes nor dislikes.
details: If the liege (`second`) is the speaker's parent, child, sibling or spouse, the neutral greeting for that relative is used. Otherwise a ceremonial regent gets the regent version, and everyone else the plain liege version.

label: Greeting to liked liege
summary: Gives the greeting to a liege the speaker likes.
details: If the liege (`second`) is the speaker's parent, child, sibling or spouse, the liked greeting for that relative is used. Otherwise a ceremonial regent gets the liked regent version, and everyone else the plain liked-liege version.

label: Greeting to lover
summary: Gives the greeting from a character to their lover.
details: Two entries. If the other person (`second`) passes the game's lover-object check, the greeting is "[titled name], my [object],". Otherwise the plain lover greeting with a pet name is used.

label: Greeting to vassal
summary: Gives the greeting the speaker uses to the other person (`second`) when that person is their vassal.
details: The checks run in this order. A parent, child, sibling or spouse gets the neutral family greeting. Then the liked greeting applies if the opinion is 30 or more, or 10 or more for a close or extended relative. An opinion of -40 or less gives the disliked greeting. Everyone else gets the plain fallback.

label: Greeting to disliked vassal
summary: Gives the greeting to a vassal the speaker dislikes, with an insult word in it.
details: Three entries. If the speaker is a ceremonial regent and the greeted person is not a ceremonial liege: "[Insult] subject of the [title],". If the speaker is a ceremonial regent and the greeted person is one: "My [insult] [title],". Otherwise "To my [insult] vassal,".

label: Greeting to neutral vassal
summary: Gives the greeting to a vassal the speaker neither likes nor dislikes.
details: A parent, child, sibling or spouse gets the neutral family greeting. Next come two versions for a speaker who is a ceremonial regent (the greeted person not a ceremonial liege, then one who is). Everyone else gets the plain vassal greeting.

label: Greeting to liked vassal
summary: Gives the greeting to a vassal the speaker likes.
details: A parent, child, sibling or spouse gets the liked family greeting. Next come two versions for a speaker who is a ceremonial regent (the greeted person not a ceremonial liege, then one who is). Then a close or extended relative gets a relative version, and everyone else the plain liked-vassal one.

label: Opening for liked ceremonial liege
summary: Gives a warm greeting such as "My [compliment word] [liege title]," to the other person (`second`).
details: Used for the case where the speaker is a ceremonial regent and the greeted person is a ceremonial liege. The title is the speaker's ceremonial liege's title, or the liege's. A speaker of the Islamic religion gets "As-salaam alaykum, my ...".

label: Opening for liked vassal
summary: Gives a warm greeting to a vassal, such as "Greetings, my [compliment word] vassal,".
details: A speaker of the Islamic religion gets the "As-salaam alaykum" form, others the plain "Greetings".

label: Opening for liked vassal, regent
summary: Gives a warm greeting such as "Greetings, [compliment word] subject of the [title],", for a speaker who is a ceremonial regent.
details: The title is the speaker's ceremonial liege's title, or the liege's. A speaker of the Islamic religion gets the "As-salaam alaykum" form, others the plain "Greetings".

label: Opening for neutral ceremonial liege
summary: Gives a neutral greeting such as "My [liege title]," to a vassal who is a ceremonial liege.
details: Used for a speaker who is a ceremonial regent. The title is the speaker's ceremonial liege's title, or the liege's. A speaker of the Islamic religion gets "As-salaam alaykum, my ...".

label: Opening for neutral vassal
summary: Gives a neutral greeting to a vassal: "To my vassal,", or "As-salaam alaykum, my vassal," for a speaker of the Islamic religion.

label: Opening for neutral vassal, regent
summary: Gives a neutral greeting such as "To the [liege's] subject,", for a speaker who is a ceremonial regent.
details: It uses the possessive form of the speaker's ceremonial liege's title, or the liege's. A speaker of the Islamic religion gets the "As-salaam alaykum" form.

label: Grit type
summary: Gives the name of the dirt-like stuff that fits the terrain where the character is: grit, dirt, sand, bog water, twigs, wet leaves or dry grass.
details: Mountains give grit (also the fallback), plains, farmlands, hills and floodplains give dirt, desert and oasis give sand, wetlands give bog water, forest and taiga give twigs, jungle gives wet leaves, and steppe and drylands give dry grass. The input shows only the first four texts.

label: Grit type, adjective
summary: Picks one of seven adjective entries by the same terrain rules as the grit type text.
details: The input shows no text for any entry, so the words are not known from it. The key is defined in the game's Polish custom-text file, and error logging is switched off for it.

label: Ground type
summary: Gives the name of the ground that fits the terrain where the character is: dirt, rocks, sandy rocks, sand, wet grass, mulch or grass.
details: Farmlands, hills and drylands give dirt, mountains rocks, desert mountains sandy rocks, desert and oasis sand, wetlands and floodplains wet grass, forest, taiga and jungle mulch, and steppe and plains grass. Dust is the fallback when nothing else fits. The input shows only the first four texts.

label: Festival animal preference
summary: Gives a phrase naming the animals a gruesome festival uses, chosen by the festival's faith.
details: It reads a faith saved on the character as `gf_faith`. Islamic faiths (and those with an Islamic syncretic rite) give clean animals such as cattle and horses, Jewish ones clean animals such as cattle, Hinduism non-sacred animals such as horses and pigs (or goats for a Hindu faith with an Islamic or Jewish rite). Pigs, cattle and horses is the fallback. The texts end with a comma.

label: Festival name
summary: Gives "blót" if the character's faith belongs to the Germanic religion, and "festival" otherwise.

label: Festival name, second form
summary: Gives "blót" if the character's faith belongs to the Germanic religion, and "festival" otherwise.
details: The entries and texts are the same as the plain festival name. It is defined in the game's Polish custom-text file; the input does not say how it differs.

label: Festival name, plural
summary: Gives "blót" if the character's faith belongs to the Germanic religion, and "festivals" otherwise.
details: The word "blót" is the same in the singular and plural forms.

label: Hand or hands
summary: Gives "hand" if the character is maimed, and "hands" otherwise.

label: A or two
summary: Gives "a " if the character is maimed, and "two" otherwise.
details: The first text ends with a space, the second does not. It is the article that goes with the hand or hands text.

label: Hated pet, singular
summary: Gives "dog" if the character has the flag `cat_person`, and "cat" if they have `dog_person`.
details: So it names the animal the character dislikes. The entries point to the game's texts for loving a dog or cat. With neither flag, no entry fits.

label: Hated pets, plural
summary: Gives "dogs" if the character has the flag `cat_person`, and "cats" if they have `dog_person`.
details: The plural of the hated pet text. With neither flag, no entry fits.

label: Health god name
summary: Gives the name of a faith's health god or figure, such as Jesus for Christianity, Chaxiraxi or Asase Yaa.
details: It runs on a faith and picks by religion or by a single faith. There are 45 entries, and the input shows the text of the first 12. It is defined in the game's Polish custom-text file.

label: Heir message
summary: Gives a sentence about an heir for the succession window, such as that the heir is underage, has no skills or has a notable trait.
details: There are 99 entries. Examples: an heir who is not an adult, one with no skill of 5 or more, one with high dread, one whose sex goes against the realm's succession law, a very skilled one, and many trait or trait-pair remarks. The texts use the heir's name with her/his and she/he words. The game may pick randomly among those that fit. The input shows only the first twelve.

label: Character introduction
summary: Gives the words that introduce the character to another person (`second`), such as "her councillor Anna".
details: Two entries that both hand over to the no-comma introduction text. The one without a comma is used when the character has a relation to the other person or holds a primary title. Otherwise the same text is used with a comma added at the end.

label: Introduction without comma
summary: Gives the way to refer to a character for another person (`second`): by her/his and a council title or relation, or as "the [relation] of ...".
details: First, a playable court chaplain councillor of `second` who is not a spouse or close family is "his [council title] [name]". Then a character with a relation to `second` is "her [relation] [titled name]". A character without a primary title is "[titled name], the spouse, father, mother, councillor or knight of ..." a ruler tied to them. A fallback text covers the rest. Eight entries in all.

label: Status towards other
summary: Gives "Vassal" if the other person (`second`) is the character's liege, "Liege" if the character is that person's liege, and "Ruler" otherwise.
details: So the word names what the character is to `second`, not their rank in general.

label: High god name
summary: Gives the name of a faith's high god, such as God, Achamán, Nyame or Dievas.
details: It runs on a faith and picks by religion or by a single faith. There are 50 entries, and the input shows the first 12 names and four texts. It is defined in the game's Polish custom-text file.

label: Historical character description
summary: Gives a short biography of a named historical person in the game, such as Omar Khayyam or Bhaskaracharya.
details: There are 208 entries. Each is chosen when the character has a variable named after the person. The texts are a few sentences about the real person's life and work. The input shows only the first twelve.

label: Historical character job
summary: Gives a short description of a historical person's role, such as "A tactful and well-liked diplomat".
details: Seventeen entries picked by the character's traits and education: eunuch, diplomat, gallant knight, strategist, warrior, explorer, soothsayer (Norse pagan mystic), theologian, monk (devoted), erudite, poet, warrior poet, banker, merchant, artist (architect), physician and author. The game may pick randomly among those that fit.

label: Roaming place name
summary: Gives a place description for a province: "[terrain] of [province]" for an empty one, or "[terrain plural] around [province]" otherwise.
details: It runs on a province. The first form is used when the province has no holding and its terrain is not farmlands, taiga or steppe. All other cases use the second. The names are written without tooltips.

label: Roaming place name, tooltip
summary: Gives the same place description as the roaming place name, but with the province name as a hoverable link.
details: It runs on a province and uses the same rules as the non-tooltip version.

label: Holding type adjective
summary: Picks an adjective entry by the holding in a province: castle, city, church, tribal, or a fallback. A province with no holding gives "No holding".
details: It runs on a province. The input shows text only for the empty case; the other entries have no text there. The key is defined in the game's Polish custom-text file.

label: Holding type adjective, yours
summary: Picks an adjective entry by the holding in a province, using the entries whose names end in _your_adj.
details: It runs on a province and has the same six cases as the plain holding adjective. The input shows text only for the empty case ("No holding"). What "your" changes in the words is not shown. It is defined in the game's Polish custom-text file.

label: Horned mythical creature
summary: Gives the name of a horned mythical creature, chosen by a variable on the character.
details: The variable is named `horned_mythical_creature` and holds a flag such as tarasque, indrik, ophiotaurus or monocerus. Ten entries in all, including centicore, erchitu, hadhayosh, bulgu, catoblepas and keewakw. The texts for the third and fourth are written "ophiotaur" and "monocer". The input shows only the first four texts.

label: Mare or stallion
summary: Gives "mare" for a female character and "stallion" for a male one.
details: It checks the character's own sex.

label: Horse story: her or him
summary: Gives "her" if the character's warhorse story has a female horse, and "him" otherwise.
details: It runs on a character and looks at the horse of the character's warhorse story (`story_cycle_martial_lifestyle_warhorse`), not at the character's own sex.

label: Horse story: her or him, any
summary: Gives "her" if the horse is female (the variable `horse_gender` is `female`), and "him" otherwise.
details: This version works on any kind of thing, such as the story itself, and reads `horse_gender` from it directly.

label: Horse story: her or his
summary: Gives "her" if the character's warhorse story has a female horse, and "his" otherwise.
details: It runs on a character and looks at the horse of the character's warhorse story, not at the character's own sex.

label: Horse story: her or his, any
summary: Gives "her" if the horse is female (the variable `horse_gender` is `female`), and "his" otherwise.
details: This version works on any kind of thing and reads `horse_gender` from it directly.

label: Horse story: mare or stallion
summary: Gives "mare" if the character's warhorse story has a female horse, and "stallion" otherwise.
details: It runs on a character and looks at the horse of the character's warhorse story.

label: Horse story: mare or stallion, any
summary: Gives "mare" if the horse is female (the variable `horse_gender` is `female`), and "stallion" otherwise.
details: This version works on any kind of thing and reads `horse_gender` from it directly.

label: Horse story: opposite mare or stallion
summary: Gives "mare" if the character's warhorse story has a male horse, and "stallion" otherwise, so it names the sex opposite to the horse's.
details: It runs on a character and looks at the horse of the character's warhorse story.

label: Opposite mare or stallion, any
summary: Gives "mare" if the horse is male (the variable `horse_gender` is `male`), and "stallion" otherwise, so it names the sex opposite to the horse's.
details: This version works on any kind of thing and reads `horse_gender` from it directly.

label: Horse story: she or he
summary: Gives "she" if the character's warhorse story has a female horse, and "he" otherwise.
details: It runs on a character and looks at the horse of the character's warhorse story, not at the character's own sex.

label: Horse story: she or he, any
summary: Gives "she" if the horse is female (the variable `horse_gender` is `female`), and "he" otherwise.
details: This version works on any kind of thing and reads `horse_gender` from it directly.

label: House of worship
summary: Gives the word for a faith's house of worship, such as church, gompa or gangging.
details: It runs on a faith and picks by religion or by a single faith, with 13 entries. The texts shown include church (Christianity), gompa (Vajrayana), gangging (Tani) and hiža (the Bosnian church). The input shows only the first four texts. It is defined in the game's Polish custom-text file.

label: Household god name, "Cel" form
summary: Picks the name of a faith's household god (or, for one faith, a wealth god) by its religion or faith.
details: It runs on a faith and has 46 entries. The input shows no text for them, so the names are not known from it. What "Cel" means is not shown. It is defined in the game's Polish custom-text file.

label: Hunt header
summary: Gives the title of a hunt: "The [character's title] Hunt" if the character has the flag `impressive_hunt`, `personal_hunt` or `glorious_hunt`, and "Hunt" otherwise.
details: The first form uses the possessive form of the character's title as a name.

label: Iberian Romance language
summary: Gives "Castilian" if the character's faith belongs to Christianity, and "Mozarabic" if it belongs to Islam.
details: For any other religion no entry fits.

label: Iberian sacred language
summary: Gives "Latin" for a Christian character, "Hebrew" for a Jewish one and "Arabic" for a Muslim one, going by the character's faith.
details: For any other religion no entry fits.
